events.title: Ennius receives Roman citizenship
events.summary: Quintus Fulvius Nobilior, son of Ennius' patron and one of the commissioners founding the citizen colonies of Potentia and Pisaurum, enrolled Ennius as a colonist, giving him Roman citizenship. Ennius commemorated it: 'nos sumus Romani qui fuimus ante Rudini' ('We are Romans, who were once men of Rudiae').

events.title: Death of Plautus
events.summary: Cicero dates the death of Titus Maccius Plautus, the Umbrian from Sarsina whose 21 surviving comedies (the canon Varro accepted) are the oldest complete works of Latin literature, to the censorship of Cato in 184. His adaptations of Greek New Comedy filled the expanding Roman festival calendar from about 205.
events.detail: Gellius preserves the story that Plautus lost his money in trade and worked in a mill, writing plays in his spare time, a tale probably constructed from his plays. Varro sifted the 130 comedies circulating under Plautus' name to 21 accepted by all, which are those that survive (the Vidularia fragmentary). Plautine comedy, with its singing slaves, inversions of the Roman household and puns in Latin on Greek settings, shows a theatre audience thoroughly familiar with Greek culture by the 190s.

events.title: War of Pharnaces I against Eumenes II
events.summary: Pharnaces I of Pontus seized Sinope in 183 and pushed into Galatia and Paphlagonia, fighting Eumenes II, Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and Prusias II. Repeated Roman embassies failed until, in 179, a peace dictated in Rome's shadow forced Pharnaces to give up his conquests except Sinope, which became the Pontic capital.
events.detail: Polybius preserves the treaty text of 179 (25.2), listing the participants, including the Sarmatian king Gatalus and the free cities of Heraclea, Mesembria, Chersonesus and Cyzicus. Rome acted only by embassies, the 'diplomacy of the Senate' that let Eumenes, its favoured client, do the fighting.

events.title: Lycortas captures Messene and avenges Philopoemen
events.summary: After the Messenian rebels executed Philopoemen in 183, his successor Lycortas besieged Messene, forced its surrender and compelled the ringleaders to kill themselves. Philopoemen's ashes were carried to Megalopolis in a solemn procession in which the young Polybius carried the urn.

events.title: Lex Orchia sumptuaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Orchius carried, with Senate backing, the first of the second-century sumptuary laws, limiting the number of guests at dinner parties. Cato spoke for it; the lex Fannia of 161 and lex Didia of 143 extended its restrictions to expenditure and to all Italy.

events.title: Aemilius Paullus defeats the Ingauni
events.summary: The proconsul Lucius Aemilius Paullus, besieged in his camp by the Ingauni Ligurians during a sham truce, broke out and routed them, killing 15,000 and capturing 2,500. The Ingauni surrendered hostages and 32 pirate ships were taken. Paullus triumphed in 181.

battle.significance: Ended Ingaunian piracy on the coast route to Massalia.

events.title: Temple of Pietas and the first gilded statue
events.summary: Manius Acilius Glabrio, son of the victor of Thermopylae, dedicated the temple of Pietas in the vegetable market vowed by his father, and set up a gilded equestrian statue of his father, the first gilded statue in Italy.

events.title: Temple of Venus Erycina outside the Colline Gate
events.summary: Lucius Porcius Licinus dedicated a second temple of Venus of Eryx, vowed by his father in the Ligurian war of 184, outside the Colline Gate. Modelled on the Sicilian sanctuary, it became associated with prostitutes, who celebrated the goddess on 23 April.

events.title: Citizen colony at Graviscae
events.summary: A citizen colony of 300 families, each receiving five iugera, was founded at Graviscae, the old port of Tarquinii and site of a Greek emporium sanctuary, on the unhealthy Etruscan coast.

events.title: Lex Baebia on the number of praetors
events.summary: A law of the consul Marcus Baebius Tamphilus provided that four and six praetors be elected in alternate years, to reduce competition for the consulship. It was soon disregarded, and six praetors were elected annually from 177.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus fights his way through the Manlian pass
events.summary: Leaving Spain with his veterans, the praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus was ambushed by Celtiberians in the Manlian pass. The Roman column, fighting in the defile, beat off the attackers, killing 17,000 by Livy's figures. Flaccus vowed a temple to Fortuna Equestris after his cavalry broke the enemy wedge.

battle.significance: Closed the First Celtiberian War's fighting season before Gracchus arrived.

events.title: Callicrates before the Senate
events.summary: Sent by the Achaean League to defend its independent handling of the Spartan exiles, Callicrates instead advised the Senate to support its friends in every Greek state and to make clear that its wishes must be obeyed. Polybius dates the beginning of Greek political degeneration under Rome from this speech.
events.detail: Polybius, himself a victim of Callicrates in 167, presents the embassy as a turning point: the Senate wrote to many Greek states urging them to back men like Callicrates, who returned home and was elected strategos. Whether Rome had a deliberate policy of building client factions or simply responded to Greek appeals is a central question in the work of Gruen and Eckstein, who stress Greek initiative, against older views (Badian) of Roman manipulation.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Derow, Rome, Polybius and the East (2015)

events.title: Philip V executes his son Demetrius
events.summary: Philip V's younger son Demetrius, former hostage and favourite of the Senate, was accused by his brother Perseus of plotting to flee to Rome and seize the throne with Roman help. After a forged letter purporting to come from Flamininus was produced, Philip had him poisoned in 180. Philip is said to have died the next year in remorse.
events.detail: Polybius treats the story as a tragedy sent by Fortune to punish Philip for his crimes (23.10). Livy's long version, with the brothers' speeches before their father, comes from him. Demetrius' embassy of 184/3 had been a diplomatic success, the Senate saying it forgave Philip for his son's sake, but this marked him as Rome's man. His death cleared the way for Perseus and fed the Roman narrative of Perseus as a usurping fratricide, used in the propaganda before the war of 171.

events.title: Latin colony at Luca
events.summary: Livy reports that the Pisans offered land for a Latin colony and that triumvirs led settlers to Luca in 180, on land taken from the Ligurians; Velleius dates Luca to 177. The colony guarded the Serchio valley route into the Apuan mountains.
events.debate: Livy's text is suspected of confusion with Luna (177); some scholars think Luca was a citizen colony or not a colony until later.

events.title: Gracchus founds Gracchurris
events.summary: After taking Complega and a string of Celtiberian towns, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus founded Gracchurris on the site of the native town of Ilurcis in the upper Ebro valley, the first Roman town named after its founder. His colleague in Ulterior, Lucius Postumius Albinus, campaigned against the Vaccaei.

events.title: Temples of Juno Regina, Diana and the Lares Permarini
events.summary: In December 179 Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, as censor, dedicated the temples of Juno Regina and Diana in the Circus Flaminius, vowed in his Ligurian war of 187, with games, and the temple of the Lares Permarini in the Campus Martius was dedicated with an inscription recording Regillus' naval victory over Antiochus.
events.detail: The tablet of the Lares Permarini, quoted by Livy, used Saturnian verse; a parallel tablet hung on the Capitol. The dedications illustrate the building programme of the censorship of 179, which also included the Basilica Aemilia (Fulvia), the piers of the Pons Aemilius and a harbour at Tarracina. The temples were set in the Circus Flaminius district, which became the showcase of triumphal monuments.

events.title: Lex Claudia de sociis and the second expulsion of Latins
events.summary: On the complaints of Latin and allied envoys, the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher carried a law requiring Latins registered at Rome since 189 to return home by 1 November. Livy describes the tricks used to gain citizenship, such as selling sons as slaves to a Roman who then freed them, and fictitious manumissions.

events.title: Ligurians capture Mutina
events.summary: In 177 the Ligurians surprised the new citizen colony of Mutina and killed its settlers. The consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher, back from Istria, retook it in three days in 176, killing 8,000 Ligurians.

events.title: Death of the consul Petillius on Mons Letum
events.summary: The consul Quintus Petillius Spurinus attacked Ligurians holding Mons Letum and the heights of Ballista. Having said in his speech that he would 'take Letum' that day, he was killed by a javelin while rallying his men. The army took the hill; the omen of 'Letum' (death) was much remarked.

battle.significance: A consul killed in action, rare in this period.

events.title: Triumph of Gracchus and the Sardinian tablet
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus triumphed over Sardinia in 175 and dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta a tablet in the shape of the island with pictures of the battles, recording that under his command over 80,000 of the enemy had been killed or captured. So many Sardinian slaves were sold that 'Sardi venales' became a proverb for cheap goods.
events.locName: Temple of Mater Matuta, Forum Boarium

events.title: Murder of Seleucus IV; Antiochus IV seizes the throne
events.summary: Seleucus IV was murdered by his chief minister Heliodorus. His brother Antiochus, just released from Rome as a hostage in exchange for Seleucus' son Demetrius and living in Athens, was escorted home by Eumenes II and Attalus, expelled Heliodorus and took the throne as Antiochus IV, at first as co-regent with Seleucus' infant son.
events.detail: An Athenian decree (OGIS 248) honours Eumenes and Attalus for installing Antiochus. Pergamon had every reason to want a friendly king in Antioch; Rome, holding Demetrius, the rightful heir, could keep the dynasty dependent. The usurpation, the boy co-ruler's murder in 170, and Demetrius' long detention set up the dynastic conflicts that fractured the Seleucid state over the next century.

events.title: Censorship of Fulvius Flaccus and Postumius Albinus
events.summary: The censors of 174 expelled nine senators, including Flaccus' own brother, and let contracts for the first paving of Rome's streets with flint (silex), gravel surfaces outside the city, the paving of the Clivus Capitolinus, a stepped approach from the Tiber to the emporium, and works in colonies such as Calatia, Auximum and Pisaurum. The census counted 269,015 citizens.
events.detail: Livy's account of the contracts (41.27) is the most detailed list of censorial public works from the Republic, showing the censors' use of revenue from the eastern wars to equip both Rome and the colonies. Postumius refused to let contracts paid by colonies without their consent, while Flaccus did so; inscriptions from Pisaurum honouring Flaccus as patron survive. The expulsion of his brother Lucius Fulvius, who had disbanded a legion without orders in Spain, illustrates censorial severity.

events.title: Pestilence of 174
events.summary: A severe epidemic struck Rome in 174, after cattle disease the year before. Livy says corpses lay unburied in the streets, the undertakers (Libitinarii) could not cope, and slaves and the poor died in great numbers; a praetor and several priests were among the dead.

events.title: The marble tiles of Juno Lacinia
events.summary: To roof his temple of Fortuna Equestris in Rome, the censor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus had half the marble roof tiles stripped from the temple of Juno Lacinia near Croton, the most venerated sanctuary of Magna Graecia. The Senate condemned the sacrilege and ordered the tiles returned, but no one could be found to replace them and they were left in the temple precinct.
events.detail: Livy presents Flaccus' later suicide (172) after news of his sons' fates as divine punishment. The episode reveals the Senate's sense of responsibility for the sanctuaries of Italy, already seen in the Pleminius affair at Locri, and the growing temptation for Roman nobles to strip Greek sites to adorn their own monuments, which the Senate tolerated outside Italy but not within it.
events.locName: Temple of Hera Lacinia, near Croton

events.title: Postumius Albinus burdens Praeneste
events.summary: The consul Lucius Postumius Albinus, offended because Praeneste had once neglected him as a private visitor, wrote ahead demanding that its magistrates meet him, provide lodging at public expense and furnish pack animals for his departure. Livy notes that no magistrate before him had imposed any charge on the allies, and that the precedent spread.
events.detail: Livy explains that magistrates had previously travelled at their own or the state's expense, with mules and tents provided from the treasury, and used private ties of hospitality (hospitium) with leading families. The episode became a classic illustration of the hardening of Roman superiority over the Italian allies in the second century, which Gaius Gracchus later dramatised with stories of magistrates flogging local officials.

events.title: Locust plague in Apulia
events.summary: Swarms of locusts from the sea covered Apulia. The praetor-elect Gnaeus Sicinius was sent with full imperium and gathered a great crowd of men to collect and destroy them, which took a long time.

events.title: Temple of Fortuna Equestris
events.summary: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus dedicated the temple of Fortuna Equestris that he had vowed in Spain in 180, celebrating four days of scenic and one day of circus games. By the reign of Tiberius the temple had disappeared.
events.locName: Near the Theatre of Pompey, Rome

events.title: Marcius Philippus' embassy and the 'new wisdom'
events.summary: Roman envoys led by Quintus Marcius Philippus met Perseus by the Peneus and induced him to accept a truce and send envoys to Rome, while Rome completed its mobilisation. Livy reports that older senators condemned this 'new wisdom' as unworthy of Roman good faith, which had once forewarned even enemies like Pyrrhus.
events.detail: Livy's contrast (42.47) between ancestral fides, which waged war openly, and the new sophistication of men who preferred deceit to courage is one of the key texts on the supposed decline of Roman morality. The majority of the Senate approved Marcius' conduct. Envoys at the same time broke up the Boeotian League, separating its cities in individual alliances with Rome.

events.title: The speech of Spurius Ligustinus
events.summary: During a dispute over the levy for the Macedonian war, former centurions demanded their old ranks. Spurius Ligustinus, a Sabine of over fifty who had inherited one iugerum and a small hut, recounted 22 years of service in Macedonia, Greece, Spain and against the Aetolians, during which he had been primus pilus four times, and declared he would serve in whatever rank the tribunes assigned. His example ended the protest.
events.detail: Livy's speech, with its six sons and two married daughters supported from one iugerum, is a celebrated, perhaps idealised, portrait of the citizen-farmer who fought Rome's overseas wars. It is used both to show the prolonged service demanded of the smallholder class (whose decline the Gracchi lamented) and, by others (Rosenstein), to argue that many such men could combine service and family farming.

events.title: Sack of Haliartus
events.summary: Haliartus, one of the Boeotian towns that stayed loyal to Perseus, was besieged by the praetor Gaius Lucretius Gallus with the fleet's crews. When it fell, the Romans killed many, sold 2,500 into slavery, carried off the statues, paintings and treasures, and razed the town; its land was later given to Athens.

battle.significance: Example of Roman severity that turned Greek opinion.

events.title: Trials over Roman misconduct in Greece
events.summary: Envoys from Chalcis complained to the Senate that Gaius Lucretius and his successor Hortensius had sacked their temples and enslaved free citizens; Abdera complained that Hortensius had executed its leaders and sold its people. The tribunes prosecuted Lucretius before the people, who fined him a million asses. The Senate ordered the enslaved Abderites freed.
events.detail: The year 170 saw a cluster of such complaints, from Chalcis, Abdera, Coronea and the Spanish provinces, and the Senate issued a decree that no one should requisition supplies from Greek communities except by its order. The senatus consultum de Thisbensibus, inscribed at Thisbe, preserves the Senate's detailed settlement of one Boeotian town the same year.

events.title: Appius Claudius defeated at Uscana
events.summary: The legate Appius Claudius Cento, operating from Lychnidus, was lured to Uscana by a promise that it would be betrayed and lost most of his 4,000 men to a sortie. In winter 170/169 Perseus himself campaigned in Illyria, took Uscana and several other towns, and opened talks with Genthius.

battle.significance: Encouraged Genthius to side with Perseus.

events.title: Senatus consultum de Thisbensibus
events.summary: A long decree of the Senate, preserved by an inscription found at Thisbe in Boeotia, settled the affairs of the town that had sided with Perseus and been taken in 171: it confirmed the property and offices of the pro-Roman faction, barred the pro-Macedonians from office for ten years, and ruled on a Thisbean woman's claims.
events.detail: The inscription (dated by the praetor Quintus Maenius, 170) is one of the best surviving texts of a senatus consultum, showing the Senate's procedure, the formulas of the decree ('quod Thisbenses verba fecerunt...') and its micro-management of a conquered community, down to grants of the right to fortify the acropolis. It illustrates how Rome rewarded its local friends and created the 'pro-Roman' parties of Greek cities.
scholarship: Sherk, Roman Documents from the Greek East (1969) no. 2

events.title: Antiochus IV invades Egypt
events.summary: When the regents of Ptolemy VI, Eulaeus and Lenaeus, prepared to reconquer Coele-Syria, Antiochus IV struck first, defeated the Ptolemaic army between Mount Casius and Pelusium, took Pelusium and overran most of Egypt, capturing his nephew Ptolemy VI. Alexandria proclaimed his brother Ptolemy VIII king and resisted.
events.detail: Antiochus claimed to act as guardian of Ptolemy VI and may have been crowned at Memphis. His second invasion in 168, when the brothers had reconciled, ended with Popillius Laenas' ultimatum at Eleusis. The Ptolemaic envoys who came to Rome in 169 begging help, and the Senate's delay until Perseus was defeated, show how the two crises were linked. Antiochus' looting of the Jerusalem temple on his way home (1 Macc 1.20-24) preceded the measures that provoked the Maccabean revolt.

events.title: Censorship of Gracchus and Claudius Pulcher
events.summary: The censors Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus and Gaius Claudius Pulcher refused contracts to the tax-farmers of the previous lustrum, provoking the tribune Publius Rutilius to prosecute them for treason; Claudius was acquitted by eight centuries. They enrolled freedmen with a son over five or a farm worth 30,000 sesterces in rural tribes and the rest in a single urban tribe, the Esquilina, chosen by lot. The census counted 312,805 citizens.
events.detail: The clash with the publicani, who had bid for the new contracts of 169 and been excluded, is the first open conflict between censors and the equestrian contractors, a group whose interests would loom large in the Gracchan age. The registration of freedmen in a single urban tribe confined their voting weight in the tribal assembly; Livy's account of the dispute between the two censors over how to do it preserves the legal argument that a censor could not deprive a citizen of his tribe without a vote of the people.

events.title: Basilica Sempronia
events.summary: The censor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus bought the house of Scipio Africanus behind the Old Shops (Veteres) near the statue of Vortumnus, with the adjacent butchers' and other shops, and built the Basilica Sempronia on the south side of the Forum. Caesar's Basilica Julia later replaced it.
events.detail: It was Rome's third basilica, after the Porcia (184) and the Fulvia/Aemilia (179); with them it framed the Forum with covered halls for business, banking and law courts. Excavations under the Basilica Julia have identified remains of the Republican structure and of earlier houses. The purchase of Africanus' house by his son-in-law is a nice instance of the elite remodelling of the Forum.
events.locName: Forum Romanum (site of the later Basilica Julia)

events.title: Aquileia reinforced with 1,500 families
events.summary: At the request of the Aquileians, who complained their colony was too weak, exposed between the Istrians and Illyrians, the Senate sent 1,500 more families under three commissioners.

events.title: Death of Ennius
events.summary: Quintus Ennius died aged 70 shortly after staging his tragedy Thyestes at the Ludi Apollinares of 169. The father of Latin poetry, he had introduced the Greek hexameter to Latin in his 18-book Annales, a verse history of Rome from Aeneas to his own day. A statue of him was said to stand in the tomb of the Scipios.
events.detail: Born at Rudiae in Calabria in 239, trilingual in Oscan, Greek and Latin (he said he had 'three hearts'), Ennius served in Sardinia, was brought to Rome by Cato in 204, and attached himself to the Scipios and Fulvii. Beyond the Annales, he wrote tragedies, comedies, satires, a didactic Euhemerus and the Hedyphagetica on gourmet fish. Only some 600 lines of the Annales survive in quotations, yet the epic shaped Roman historical memory until Virgil; Cicero quoted it constantly, and lines such as 'moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque' became proverbial.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Quintus Ennius (1985)
Goldberg and Manuwald, Fragmentary Republican Latin I (2018)

events.title: Scipio Nasica turns the Elpeus line at Pythium
events.summary: Facing Perseus' fortified line on the Elpeus, Aemilius Paullus sent Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica (later Corculum) with 8,000 picked troops over the mountain via Pythium by night. Nasica overcame a Macedonian detachment under Milo near the pass, forcing Perseus to abandon the river line and fall back to Pydna.

battle.significance: Forced the battle of Pydna on open ground.

events.debate: Plutarch had Nasica's own letter describing the march; Polybius gave smaller numbers for the Macedonian detachment.

events.title: Porticus Octavia
events.summary: Gnaeus Octavius, who took Perseus' surrender at Samothrace and triumphed at sea in 167, built a double colonnade near the Circus Flaminius with bronze Corinthian capitals, called the Porticus Corinthia. Augustus rebuilt it, keeping the name, after 33 BC.

events.title: Crates of Mallos lectures in Rome
events.summary: The Pergamene scholar Crates of Mallos, sent as envoy by Attalus (II) around the time of Ennius' death, fell into an opening of the sewer on the Palatine and broke his leg. During his convalescence he gave frequent lectures, which Suetonius calls the beginning of the study of grammar and literary criticism at Rome.
events.debate: Suetonius dates it 'between the second and third Punic Wars, about the time of Ennius' death'; 168 or 159 have been proposed.

events.title: The Galatians attack Pergamon; Rome declares them free
events.summary: In 168 the Galatians, encouraged by Prusias II and by Rome's coolness towards Eumenes II, invaded the Pergamene kingdom. Eumenes defeated them by 166, but the Senate, which suspected him of double dealing with Perseus, declared the Galatians autonomous, provided they stayed within their own borders.

events.title: Cato's Origines
events.summary: In old age Cato wrote the Origines, seven books in Latin covering the foundation legends of Rome and the cities of Italy (books 1-3) and the wars from the First Punic War to 149 (books 4-7). It named no generals, calling them 'the consul' or 'the dictator', but did name the elephant Surus, and included Cato's own speeches.
events.detail: The Origines was the first history of Rome in Latin and a deliberate counterpart to the Greek-language histories of Fabius Pictor and Postumius Albinus. Its interest in the origins of Italian communities reflected a vision of Roman history as the history of Italy. Only fragments survive, including the heroic stand of a military tribune (Caedicius or Calpurnius Flamma) in 258 and the speeches for the Rhodians (167) and against Galba (149).

events.title: Prusias II prostrates himself before the Senate
events.summary: Prusias II of Bithynia came to Rome to congratulate the Senate on Pydna, wearing a shaven head, white cap and toga like a newly freed slave, called himself the freedman of the Roman people, kissed the threshold of the Senate house and hailed the senators as saviour gods. Polybius found the performance disgusting, but it served Prusias well.

events.title: Triumph of Anicius and the Greek musicians
events.summary: Lucius Anicius Gallus triumphed over Genthius and the Illyrians. At his victory games he brought the best Greek pipers and dancers onto a stage in the circus, then, finding their performance dull, ordered them through a lictor to fight; the musicians turned the concert into a mock battle, to the crowd's delight. Polybius' account is a classic text on Roman taste.

events.title: Cato's speech for the Rhodians
events.summary: When a praetor proposed war on Rhodes for its attempt to mediate between Rome and Perseus, Cato, aged 67, spoke against it in the Senate. Fragments preserved by Gellius argue that the Rhodians should not be punished for wishes rather than deeds, and that Roman good fortune should not make the Senate arrogant. War was averted, but Rhodes lost Lycia and Caria.
events.detail: The speech was included in Cato's Origines, book 5, and is the longest surviving piece of Republican oratory before Gracchus and Cicero. Tiro, Cicero's freedman, criticised it, and Gellius defends it at length. Its argument from Roman self-interest ('we too would not wish to be punished for wanting something') shows Cato as a pragmatic opponent of naked aggression, not the simple hawk of the Carthage debate. Rhodes received a formal alliance only in 164.

events.title: The Maccabean revolt begins
events.summary: After Antiochus IV's officials turned the Jerusalem temple into a sanctuary of Zeus Olympios (December 167) and banned circumcision and the Sabbath, the priest Mattathias killed a Jew sacrificing on a pagan altar and a royal officer at Modein and took to the hills with his sons. Under Judas Maccabaeus the revolt defeated several Seleucid armies.
events.detail: The causes are debated: the sources present a religious persecution, but modern accounts (Bickerman, Tcherikover, Gruen) stress a civil conflict between Hellenising high priests (Jason, Menelaus) and traditionalists, Antiochus' need for money after Eleusis, and his punishment of a Jerusalem that had rebelled while he was in Egypt. The revolt was the start of the Hasmonean state, which sought Roman friendship in 161 and became Rome's client a century later.
scholarship: Bickerman, The God of the Maccabees (1937; Eng. 1979)

events.title: The procession of Antiochus IV at Daphne
events.summary: Antiochus IV staged a festival at Daphne to outdo Aemilius Paullus' games at Amphipolis. Polybius describes a parade of 50,000 troops, including 5,000 men armed 'in the Roman fashion', 36 elephants, chariots, 800 ephebes in gold crowns and endless gold and silver vessels, with the king himself acting as master of ceremonies and clown.
events.detail: The review is the best evidence for the Seleucid army after Apamea and shows that the treaty limits on elephants were flouted (hence Gnaeus Octavius' mission of 163-162). The legionary-style unit suggests Hellenistic armies experimenting with Roman equipment. Polybius' hostile portrait of Antiochus 'Epimanes' (the mad) comes from the same section.

events.title: Eumenes II turned away at Brundisium
events.summary: Suspected of having negotiated with Perseus, Eumenes II sailed to Italy in winter 167/6 to defend himself. The Senate, not wishing to receive or openly rebuff its oldest ally, decreed that no king should come to Rome, and a quaestor met Eumenes at Brundisium to tell him to leave Italy.

events.title: The Great Altar of Pergamon
events.summary: Under Eumenes II the Pergamenes built the Great Altar on the acropolis, with a 113-metre frieze of the battle of the gods and giants, an allegory of Attalid victories over the Galatians, and an inner frieze of the story of Telephus, mythical founder of Pergamon. Its remains are in Berlin.
events.debate: Dating ranges from c. 180 to after 166; some link it to Eumenes' Galatian victory of 166, others to the 180s. The Ampelius notice of a great marble altar is the only literary reference.

events.title: Ptolemy VI comes to Rome as a refugee
events.summary: Expelled from Alexandria by his brother Ptolemy VIII, Ptolemy VI arrived in Rome with a few attendants and lodged with an Alexandrian painter in a garret, refusing the ostentatious welcome offered by Demetrius, the Seleucid hostage. The Senate restored him and in 163 divided the kingdom: Egypt and Cyprus to Philometor, Cyrenaica to Euergetes.

events.title: Death of Antiochus IV in Persis
events.summary: Campaigning in the eastern satrapies to restore Seleucid authority and raise money, Antiochus IV failed in an attempt to plunder a temple of Nanaia/Artemis in Elymais and died of illness at Tabae in Persis in late 164. A Babylonian king list records the news of his death in the month Kislev. His nine-year-old son Antiochus V succeeded under the regent Lysias.

events.title: Census of 164: 337,022 citizens
events.summary: The censors Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Quintus Marcius Philippus registered 337,022 citizens, the highest figure before the Gracchan census of 125.
events.debate: The decline to 328,316 (159), 324,000 (154) and 317,933 (136) has been read as evidence of rural impoverishment (the Gracchan diagnosis) or of evasion of registration to avoid the levy.

events.title: Rhodes obtains a treaty of alliance with Rome
events.summary: After two years of humiliating embassies following its loss of Caria and Lycia, Rhodes was granted a formal treaty of alliance (foedus) with Rome, something it had always avoided in order to remain free of entanglements. The terms bound Rhodes to have the same friends and enemies as Rome.

events.title: Rededication of the Jerusalem temple (Hanukkah)
events.summary: On 25 Kislev (December) 164, three years after its desecration, Judas Maccabaeus' forces purified the temple, rebuilt the altar and resumed the sacrifices, a festival commemorated annually as Hanukkah. A letter preserved in 2 Maccabees shows Roman envoys, Quintus Memmius and Titus Manlius, offering to support Jewish requests to the regent Lysias the same year.
events.debate: The authenticity of the letter of the Roman envoys (2 Macc 11.34-38) is debated; if genuine it is the earliest Roman contact with the Maccabees.

events.title: Juventius Thalna dies of joy
events.summary: The consul Manius Juventius Thalna, having subdued Corsica, was offering sacrifice when he received the Senate's letter decreeing a thanksgiving in his honour; he read it, collapsed and died at the altar. Valerius Maximus and Pliny cite him as the classic case of death from sudden joy.

events.title: The consuls of 162 abdicate over a flaw in the auspices
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, presiding over the elections for 162, realised later, while governor of Sardinia, that he had crossed the pomerium and re-entered without retaking the auspices. He wrote to the augurs; the consuls he had returned, Publius Scipio Nasica Corculum and Gaius Marcius Figulus, were recalled from their provinces and abdicated.
events.detail: Cicero uses the case as the model of scrupulous respect for augural law, set against Gracchus' earlier anger when the haruspices had first questioned the election. It shows how procedural flaws (vitium) could annul elections and how the augural college held real constitutional power, a power used politically in the following century.

events.title: Murder of Gnaeus Octavius at Laodicea
events.summary: Gnaeus Octavius, sent with two colleagues to enforce the Apamea treaty on the boy king Antiochus V, had the Seleucid warships burned and the war elephants hamstrung. A man named Leptines murdered him in the gymnasium at Laodicea. The Senate honoured him with a statue on the Rostra but took no revenge.
events.detail: Demetrius, the Seleucid hostage in Rome, used the crisis to ask again to be released. When refused, he escaped with Polybius' help and seized the throne (162), sending Leptines to Rome for punishment. The Senate refused to accept the murderer, a calculated refusal to absolve the new king. The episode shows Rome's willingness to impose disarmament clauses by bare authority and the risks its envoys ran.

events.title: Terence's Eunuchus: the most profitable Roman comedy
events.summary: Terence's Eunuchus, adapted from Menander, was such a success at the Ludi Megalenses of 161 that it was performed twice in one day, and the aediles paid 8,000 sesterces for it, the highest fee recorded for a comedy. His Phormio followed at the Ludi Romani the same year.

events.title: Funeral games of Aemilius Paullus: Terence's Adelphoe and Hecyra
events.summary: At the funeral games for Lucius Aemilius Paullus, given by his sons Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Maximus Aemilianus, Terence's Adelphoe was produced and the Hecyra was staged for the second time; it failed again when the audience left for a gladiatorial show. A third attempt later that year succeeded.
events.detail: The Hecyra prologues are unique evidence for the competitive conditions of the Roman stage: the first performance (165) was ruined by a tightrope walker and boxers, the second (160) by a rumour of gladiators. The Adelphoe, a debate between strict and indulgent fathers, has been read as reflecting the Scipionic household's own discussions of Greek education.

sources.r: Adelphoe and Hecyra didascaliae and prologues

events.title: Cato's De agri cultura
events.summary: Around 160 Cato wrote his manual on farming, the oldest complete work of Latin prose. It describes a medium-sized estate of the new type, with a vineyard of 100 iugera worked by 16 slaves and an olive grove of 240 iugera by 13, gives recipes for cakes, medicine and contracts, and advises selling old and sick slaves.
events.detail: The work is a jumble of instructions rather than a treatise, but it is fundamental evidence for the market-oriented slave villa of central Italy in the generation after the Hannibalic war, the 'villa system' later excavated at sites like Settefinestre. Cato's estates were in Latium and Campania (Casinum, Venafrum); he also invested in pasture, fishponds and maritime loans through a freedman. The contrast with the smallholder ideal Cato celebrated in his speeches has fascinated historians.
scholarship: Marzano, Roman Villas in Central Italy (2007)

events.title: Death of Terence
events.summary: Publius Terentius Afer, the African-born freedman whose six comedies all survive, left Rome after 160 for Greece, reportedly to collect more plays of Menander, and died in 159, perhaps at sea or in Arcadia, still in his mid-twenties to mid-thirties. Rumour held that his noble friends Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius had helped write his plays.

events.title: Lex Cornelia Fulvia de ambitu
events.summary: The consuls of 159, Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, carried a law against electoral bribery that, according to the Livian epitome, imposed penalties on those convicted, the second such statute after the lex Cornelia Baebia of 181; its precise penalties are uncertain.

events.title: The Macedonian gold and silver mines reopened
events.summary: Aemilius Paullus had closed the royal gold and silver mines of Macedonia in 167, leaving only copper and iron, so that neither the publicani nor the four new republics would profit from them. In 158 the Senate allowed the mines to be reopened; the four Macedonian republics struck large silver tetradrachm issues.
events.detail: Livy reports that the Senate feared that if the mines were let to the publicani the allies would lose their freedom, and if worked by the Macedonians, the profits would fund sedition. The reversal of 158 coincides with a large increase in Roman denarius output in the 150s.

events.title: Citizen colony at Auximum
events.summary: Velleius dates the colony of Auximum in Picenum to 157, the last citizen colony in Italy before the Gracchan foundations; the censors of 174 had already paid for walls and shops there.

events.title: War of Prusias II against Attalus II
events.summary: Prusias II invaded the Pergamene kingdom, besieged Pergamon, burned the Nicephorium sanctuary and plundered temples. After a series of Roman embassies were ignored, the Senate threatened war; in 154 Prusias agreed to pay 500 talents in instalments and to hand back 20 decked ships.

events.title: Second Cretan War
events.summary: Rhodes fought a second war against Cretan cities that had raided Rhodian territory, losing a naval battle off Siphnos and appealing to the Achaeans, who refused help on Roman advice. Rome mediated an end without decisive result, a sign of the decline of Rhodian naval power.

events.title: Opimius campaigns for Massalia against the Oxybii and Deciates
events.summary: At the request of Massalia, whose colonies Antipolis and Nicaea were attacked by the Ligurian Oxybii and Deciates, who had also wounded Roman envoys, the consul Quintus Opimius crossed the Alps by the coast, defeated both peoples and gave their land to the Massaliots. It was Rome's first campaign in what became Gallia Narbonensis.

battle.significance: First Roman intervention beyond the Alps.

events.title: Lusitanians under Caesarus defeat Mummius
events.summary: After the Lusitanian leader Punicus was killed, his successor Caesarus defeated the praetor Lucius Mummius (the future destroyer of Corinth), killing 9,000 Romans and capturing the camp and standards, which were paraded through Celtiberia. Mummius recovered with a smaller success later.

events.title: Marcellus makes peace with the Celtiberians
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul for the third time, took Ocilis and Nertobriga with moderation and persuaded the Belli, Titthi and Arevaci to send envoys to Rome. The Senate, urged by the hawks, rejected the peace, but Marcellus concluded a settlement on the Gracchan terms with a payment of 600 talents before his successor Lucullus arrived.
events.detail: Polybius (35.2-3) describes the Senate's reception of the Celtiberian envoys and the Roman aristocrats who wanted war for glory, alongside the young men who evaded the levy. Marcellus was accused of being bribed; the peace held with the Arevaci until 143. It shows the senatorial division between negotiated settlement and wars of annihilation that ran through the Spanish wars.

events.title: Siege of Intercatia and Aemilianus' single combat
events.summary: After the massacre at Cauca, Lucullus besieged the Vaccaean town of Intercatia. The young military tribune Scipio Aemilianus accepted a challenge from a Spanish champion and killed him, and was first over the wall when it was breached, winning the mural crown. Aemilianus negotiated the town's surrender; Lucullus failed at Pallantia.

events.title: Alexander Balas defeats and kills Demetrius I
events.summary: Alexander Balas, presented as a son of Antiochus IV, recognised by the Roman Senate in 153/2 and backed by Attalus II, Ptolemy VI and Jonathan Maccabaeus, landed at Ptolemais and in 150 defeated Demetrius I, who died fighting heroically. Balas married Ptolemy's daughter Cleopatra Thea.

battle.significance: Seleucid succession settled by a pretender acknowledged by Rome.

events.title: Release of the Achaean exiles
events.summary: After sixteen years in Italy, the surviving Achaean detainees, about 300 of the original 1,000, were allowed home after Scipio Aemilianus lobbied for them and Cato asked whether the Senate had nothing better to do than debate whether Greek old men should be buried by Roman or Achaean undertakers. Polybius, wanting his honours restored, was told by Cato he was like Odysseus going back into the Cyclops' cave for his cap.
events.detail: The returnees included embittered opponents of Rome, among them men who later led the Achaean League into the war of 146. Polybius himself spent the following years with Scipio, at Carthage in 147-146 and in the settlement of Greece in 146-145.

events.title: Trial of Servius Sulpicius Galba
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Scribonius Libo proposed a special court to try Servius Sulpicius Galba for his massacre of the surrendered Lusitanians. Cato, in his last year, spoke for the bill. Galba escaped by bringing his young sons and orphaned ward before the people in tears, and the assembly rejected it.
events.detail: Cicero, who had read Galba's speeches, admired him as the first Roman orator to use digressions and appeals to the emotions. The failure of the prosecution prompted the lex Calpurnia of the same year, setting up a permanent court for provincial extortion. Galba, enriched by Lusitanian spoil, went on to the consulship of 144. The case is a prime example of the impunity of Roman commanders for atrocities against provincials.

events.title: Nicomedes II overthrows Prusias II
events.summary: Prusias II sent his son Nicomedes to Rome and planned to have him murdered there. Warned, Nicomedes allied with Attalus II, invaded Bithynia, and Prusias, abandoned by his subjects, was killed in the temple of Zeus at Nicomedia. A Roman embassy sent to mediate, its members a gouty, a scarred and a foolish man, prompted Cato's quip that it had neither feet, head nor heart.

events.title: First battle of Nepheris
events.summary: The consul Manius Manilius marched against the Carthaginian field army under Hasdrubal at Nepheris and was beaten in a river crossing. Scipio Aemilianus, a military tribune, saved four trapped cohorts with the cavalry and recovered the bodies of the fallen tribunes, enhancing his reputation.

battle.significance: Made Scipio Aemilianus the hope of the army.

events.title: Andriscus destroys the praetor Juventius
events.summary: After Andriscus, the pretended son of Perseus, had made himself king in Macedonia and invaded Thessaly, the praetor Publius Juventius Thalna marched against him with one legion and was killed with most of his army, the only time a Roman praetorian army was destroyed in the Greek East.

battle.significance: Brought Metellus and a consular-scale response.

events.title: Calpurnius Piso fails at Hippo Diarrhytus
events.summary: The consul Lucius Calpurnius Piso, avoiding Carthage itself, attacked the towns of its hinterland; he failed at Clupea and besieged Hippo Diarrhytus all summer, losing his siege engines to sorties, while the Carthaginians grew bold and Masinissa's son Gulussa grew cool.

battle.significance: The low point of the Roman siege effort.

events.title: Death of Masinissa; his kingdom divided
events.summary: Masinissa died aged about 90, having ruled the Massylii and then all Numidia for over half a century. On his request Scipio Aemilianus divided the royal powers among his three legitimate sons: Micipsa received the capital Cirta and the treasury, Gulussa the army, Mastanabal the administration of justice.
events.detail: Polybius' obituary credits Masinissa with turning Numidia from nomadism to settled agriculture, which the archaeology of the period partly supports, and remarks that he fathered a son at 86 and could still ride all day. The tumulus of Le Medracen and the monument at El Khroub (possibly Masinissa's tomb) illustrate Numidian royal display. The triple division kept Numidia weak and dependent; Micipsa outlived his brothers and left the kingdom to his sons and his nephew Jugurtha.

events.title: Construction of the Via Postumia
events.summary: The consul Spurius Postumius Albinus Magnus built the Via Postumia across northern Italy from Genua over the Apennines to Dertona, Placentia, Cremona, Verona and Aquileia, linking the Ligurian coast to the head of the Adriatic. A milestone found near Genua bears his name.
events.locName: Cisalpine Gaul from Genua to Aquileia

events.title: Aemilianus storms Megara
events.summary: Arriving as consul, Scipio Aemilianus restored discipline, expelled camp followers, and launched a night attack on Megara, the garden suburb of Carthage. His men got onto a tower and opened a gate; the defenders fled to the Byrsa. Hasdrubal answered by torturing Roman prisoners on the walls in view of the besiegers.

battle.significance: Gave Rome a foothold inside the city walls.

events.title: The Carthaginian fleet breaks out
events.summary: When Scipio blocked the harbour entrance with a great mole, the Carthaginians secretly cut a new channel to the sea from the inner harbour and launched a fleet of about 50 triremes built from old timber. They failed to attack at once; when they did, they fought the Roman fleet all day but lost many ships in the return through the narrow channel.
events.detail: Excavations of the circular military harbour (the cothon) at Carthage have revealed shipsheds for some 170 to 180 vessels around an island admiralty, and a channel matching Appian's account. The episode is a testimony to Carthaginian ingenuity in the last siege.

events.title: Aurelius Orestes' embassy at Corinth
events.summary: In summer 147 a Roman embassy under Lucius Aurelius Orestes told the Achaean assembly at Corinth that Sparta, Corinth, Argos, Heraclea near Oeta and Arcadian Orchomenus should be detached from the League. The crowd rioted and attacked Spartans in the city; Orestes reported that his embassy had been insulted. A second, milder embassy under Sextus Julius Caesar failed.
events.detail: Whether Rome intended to break up the League (Pausanias, Justin) or Orestes exceeded his instructions is debated; Polybius blames the demagogues Critolaus and Diaeus and the 'madness' of the masses. The episode moved the conflict from a quarrel over Sparta to war with Rome, ended by Mummius at Corinth.
